uncited: Space Warping (Log+Warp) is a coordinate transformation technique used in neural volume rendering to improve the efficiency of positional encoding by adapting the sampling density to the scene's depth structure.

It solves the problem where standard positional encodings struggle to represent high-frequency details in the foreground while simultaneously handling low-frequency background variations, as the background occupies a disproportionately large volume in Euclidean space.

It sets itself apart from its parent [Interpolation and Sampling Techniques](2787-interpolation-and-sampling-techniques.md) by explicitly warping the 3D coordinate space before encoding, and from its sibling [NDC Warping](7267-ndc-warping.md) by using a radial distortion function rather than a linear NDC squash, making it suitable for general forward-facing scenes rather than strictly planar or specific trajectory constraints.
The method combines logarithmic depth sampling with a radial space warping function to compress the background into the foreground region of the encoding space.

where $|\mathbf{p}|$ is the Euclidean norm of the relative position vector, and $d_{max}$ is the maximum depth of the scene or view frustum.

It is chosen when multi-view consistency is critical and multiple camera poses are available for training.
- **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ per sample for the warping calculation, assuming constant-time positional encoding.
- **Memory Complexity**: $O(1)$ additional memory per sample for storing the warped coordinate.
- **Strengths**: Reduces the bandwidth required for positional encoding to represent large depth ranges; aligns with natural image statistics.
It builds on the observation that background details are naturally lower frequency, similar to mip-mapped textures.
The method combines logarithmic depth sampling with a radial warping function to optimize the input distribution to the neural network.
